checks.title: Scope
checks.detail: We set the time window to cover the incident.

checks.title: Signal
checks.detail: We filtered with a query to find the records behind the report.

checks.title: Evidence
checks.detail: We opened one matching event to confirm what the query found.

answer.evidence: The KQL result and expanded event connect ${var.finding_phrase} to ${truth.scope}.

goals.title: Set the time window
goals.concept: Setting a time range separates the incident from everyday, background activity.
goals.narration: The report says the problem was first noticed at ${incident.noticed_clock} (${incident.noticed_ago}). Set a time window that starts a little before then, without pulling in much older traffic.
goals.reasoning: A short time range keeps the incident in view. Older data from normal times would only confuse the comparison.
goals.evidence: The histogram and results should refresh to the window you picked.

demonstration.narration: The problem was noticed at ${incident.noticed_clock}. I'll start the window at ${incident.window_start_clock}, the five-minute mark before it. That moment then stays in view, however long we take.
demonstration.evidence: The histogram and hit count now start at ${incident.window_start_clock}. The report at ${incident.noticed_clock} sits inside the window, and older traffic is left out of the comparison.

drifts.note: You started searching before setting the time window; this step is about choosing when to look.

hints: Too short a window misses the report entirely; a much longer one mixes older, normal traffic into the comparison.
Click the date box at the top of Discover. Type a start date and time, then “to now”. Or drag across the histogram. A fixed start stays where it is while you investigate.
Start the window at ${incident.window_start_clock}: type “${incident.window_start_typed} to now”. Show me can do it for you.

goals.title: Find the records that matter
goals.concept: A query should narrow the evidence without assuming more than the brief tells you.
goals.narration: Narrow the results to the records behind the report. Filter or query the field that sets them apart from normal traffic.
goals.reasoning: Filtering on the key field separates the unusual records from the normal ones, so you can compare them.
goals.evidence: The results that remain show the problem.

demonstration.narration: I'll filter on ${var.field} to focus on the records linked to the reported problem.
demonstration.reasoning: The window holds normal events as well as the problem. Filtering on ${var.field} removes that noise, so we can look at the records that matter.
demonstration.evidence: The query bar now holds the filter, and the hit count shows how many records match it. Next, we'll open one of them.

hints: Find the field that sets the unusual records apart.

Type a query in the KQL bar. Join conditions with and, or, not and parentheses. Use * as a wildcard, and field:* to check that a field has a value. Or use Add filter, or the + and − next to a value in a field's Top values.
Filter on ${var.field}; Show me can enter a reference query.

goals.title: Check the evidence in one event
goals.concept: A conclusion is stronger when you open one typical event and check it.
goals.narration: Open one typical result and read the fields that back up the finding. To keep a field at the top, point at its row and click the pin icon at the left of it.
goals.reasoning: Checking a single event stops you from drawing a conclusion from totals alone.
goals.evidence: The event you open contains the facts that back up the finding.

demonstration.narration: I'll open one matching event to check the key fields together. A result count alone can't show whether they occur in the same request.
demonstration.reasoning: A total can look convincing even when it includes other records. Opening one typical event shows the key values together, which a count alone can't do.
demonstration.evidence: This one event shows ${truth.finding} together with ${truth.scope}, not just in a total. That supports the conclusion: ${truth.conclusion}

drifts.note: You added ${action.field} as a column; this step checks ${var.field} across rows, or one whole event.

hints: Check one typical record instead of relying only on the count.

Expand a row (the ⤢ at its left) to read all of its fields in the panel on the right. To keep a field at the top, click the pin icon at the left of its row. Or add ${var.field} as a column to compare it across rows.
Open the first result; Show me can do it for you.

goals.title: Submit a conclusion you can back up
goals.concept: A good answer states the finding, its scope, and the evidence that links them.
goals.narration: Write down the conclusion and point to the evidence for it.
goals.reasoning: The answer should keep what you saw separate from what you worked out.
goals.evidence: The answer points to the signal and the event that backs it up.
hints: Sum up what the evidence shows.
Use the coach's answer form: name what you found, its scope, and what the evidence shows.
Submit the finding, scope and conclusion; Show me shows the reference summary.
